solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: In time, gastarbeiter's a household name!

indicators.note: 'in' tells you the answer sits inside the run of letters that follows

parts.note: read straight across the end of one word into the start of the next, ignoring the comma

explanation.surface: A guest worker from Germany becomes famous given enough time.
explanation.walkthrough: A gastarbeiter is a German guest worker, which makes the surface read like a success story. The answer runs from the tail of 'time' into 'gastarbeiter'.
explanation.definitionFit: A megastar is someone so famous that everybody knows their name, which is exactly what a household name is.

clue.text: Monsieur did fish, and so did butcher

definitions.note: a verb here; with the 'did' before it, it means butchered, the past tense the answer has

parts.note: M. is the French abbreviation for Monsieur
to angle is to fish with rod and line

explanation.surface: A Frenchman went fishing, and so did the local butcher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher' looks like a person, the second fisherman; it is a verb, and 'did butcher' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To mangle something is to hack it about and ruin it, which is what butchering a job or a text means figuratively.

clue.text: Acquired grand place for Ruth and Samuel

parts.note: G is the standard abbreviation for grand
the books of Ruth and Samuel are in the Old Testament, abbreviated OT

explanation.surface: Someone bought an impressive home for a couple called Ruth and Samuel.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruth and Samuel sound like people buying a house, but they are books of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Got is the past tense of get, meaning obtained or came into possession of something.

clue.text: After interference, fail in move to stop slide?

indicators.note: one thing coming after another puts the pieces in sequence, second behind first

parts.note: snow is the speckled interference on an untuned analogue TV screen
to plough is British slang for failing an exam

explanation.surface: Someone flunks an attempt to halt a slide after being meddled with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plough' meaning to fail an exam is dated British student slang. The question mark flags that the definition is a skiing term.
explanation.definitionFit: In skiing, the snowplough is a manoeuvre with ski tips pointed together to brake and stop a downhill slide.

clue.text: Expect answers when buttonholing head of intelligence

indicators.note: something at the head goes in front, so one piece leads the rest
to buttonhole someone is to grab and hold them, so one piece holds another

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for answer; two answers give two of them
wit means intelligence or mental sharpness

explanation.surface: You should expect replies when you corner the spy chief.
explanation.walkthrough: One A goes at the head and the other is held inside WIT. 'Head of intelligence' reads as a spymaster, but it is positional.
explanation.definitionFit: To await something is to wait for it and anticipate its arrival, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Didn't manage everything, finishing early delivery

indicators.note: finishing early means stopping before the end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: someone who managed only part of something ran some of it

explanation.surface: A courier who could not complete the round finished early.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivery' looks like a parcel round; it is rescue. RAN means managed, as in running a business.
explanation.definitionFit: Delivery can mean release from captivity, and a ransom is the price paid to secure that release, so this is a sense stretch.

clue.text: Maybe old Bill's John's successor

definitions.meaning: a bill passed into law becomes an act, so old bills include these
the book that follows John's gospel in the New Testament

explanation.walkthrough: Old Bill is British slang for the police, which sends you looking for policemen; here it is just a former parliamentary bill. The 's is 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Laws passed by Parliament are statutes that began life as bills, and the fifth New Testament book comes straight after the Gospel of John.

clue.text: Be as one initially scared by series of echoes — then you kick yourself?

indicators.note: 'then' means next in sequence, so what follows is added on after
'initially' points to the opening letter of the next word only

parts.note: the opening letter
Echo is E in the NATO phonetic alphabet, and a series gives three
ye is the old form of you
to toe a ball is to kick it with the tip of the foot
ye again, the archaic you

explanation.surface: Someone startled by a string of echoes kicks themselves in frustration.
explanation.walkthrough: The last phrase is read word by word: you, kick, yourself, giving YE TOE YE.
explanation.definitionFit: To see eye to eye is an idiom meaning to agree completely, which is to be united in opinion.

clue.text: Go immediately after this long-range spring forecast

definitions.meaning: on a British Monopoly board, the GO square comes straight after the most expensive property
a weather prediction made well ahead for a month in spring, read as two words

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' looks like an instruction; it is the Monopoly square. Mayfair is the priciest square on the UK Monopoly board, sitting just before GO.
explanation.definitionFit: The London district is the final Monopoly square before GO, and split in two it predicts good weather for the fifth month of the year.

clue.text: Line in cookery books, maybe, was intensely illuminating

definitions.note: a past-tense verb phrase; the answer is the past tense of floodlight

indicators.note: one thing placed in another sits inside it

parts.note: books about cooking are food literature, lit for short
L is the abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A sentence in a cookbook shed a brilliant light on the subject.
explanation.walkthrough: The L goes in just after the F. 'Maybe' marks cookery books as one example of food literature.
explanation.definitionFit: To floodlight is to light brightly with powerful lamps, and its past tense describes having done so.

clue.text: Raving intolerantly to a sponsor of good causes

indicators.note: raving is wild and disordered, so the letters are thrown about

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone rants bigotedly at a charitable benefactor.
explanation.walkthrough: The UK National Lottery gives part of its takings to good causes such as arts, sport and heritage.
explanation.definitionFit: The British state lottery funds charities and community projects, so it describes itself as a sponsor of worthy causes.

clue.text: Nothing sailor can do ultimately stops preparation for it

indicators.note: something that stops a gap plugs it, sitting inside it

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring
PO is a Petty Officer
a tin is a can

indicators.note: 'ultimately' means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: However hard a sailor tries, nothing helps him get ready for the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' is a coy crossword word for sex, so the preparation is one that stirs desire. The O plugs TIN between its I and N.
explanation.definitionFit: A love potion is a magic brew meant to make someone amorous, so it is a preparation made for romance and sex.

clue.text: Vintage rite involved sharp dressing

indicators.note: involved means tangled and complicated, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An old ceremony required participants to dress smartly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sharp dressing' suggests smart clothes; it is a tangy salad dressing.
explanation.definitionFit: Vinaigrette is an oil and vinegar salad sauce, and the vinegar gives it an acidic, tart taste.

clue.text: Girl who's got people gunning for me?

parts.note: something for me is mine, my own
the Royal Artillery, the British Army's gunners

explanation.surface: A woman laments that she has people out to get her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gunning for me' sounds like being targeted; it is literally my own gunners, a regiment belonging to me.
explanation.definitionFit: Myra is a female first name, and crosswords routinely use girl to clue any woman's given name.

clue.text: Musical, variable one, about Perth hospital area nurses

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close in the arms, so one piece holds another

parts.note: a hospital area is a ward, and Perth is in Australia, Oz

indicators.note: turning about means facing the other way, so the pair is read backwards

parts.note: algebra uses letters such as x, y and z for variables
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A changeable person puts on a show about nurses in an Australian hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: Perth here is the city in Western Australia, not the Scottish one; Oz is informal for Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wizard of Oz is the famous film musical, with several stage versions as well.

clue.text: Tries, in the front row, for Australian pack

indicators.note: being in the front means leading, so one piece is placed before the other

parts.note: a din is a loud row, a racket
has a go, attempts

explanation.surface: Rugby tries scored by the front-row forwards for an Australian team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Front row' and 'tries' paint a rugby scene, but row is noise and tries are attempts.
explanation.definitionFit: Dingoes are wild dogs native to Australia, and they hunt in packs, so a group of them is an Australian pack.

clue.text: Stash stuff in cellar, above a street

indicators.note: in a down answer, what is above comes first

parts.note: a salt cellar is a small table container for salt
a street is a way, as in Broadway

explanation.surface: Hide your belongings down in the basement, over the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cellar' suggests a basement; it is the salt cellar on the dining table.
explanation.definitionFit: To salt away money or goods is an idiom for hoarding them secretly for later, as preserved food was once stored.

clue.text: Surgeon grabs tip of nice long pointed object

indicators.note: to grab is to seize and hold, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: Joseph Lister, the pioneer of antiseptic surgery

indicators.note: a tip is an end, here the far end, so only the final letter is used

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: A surgeon takes hold of the end of a nice long instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: Lister is the Victorian surgeon who introduced antiseptics; the E slips in after his first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A leister is a multi-pronged fishing spear, which is a long pointed weapon for catching salmon.

clue.text: This used to set Raleigh off on travels

indicators.note: setting off on travels moves things about, so the letters wander into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Sir Walter Raleigh used to be sent off on voyages of exploration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set' reads as sending Raleigh off; in the definition it means fixing a hairstyle.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair gel is a styling product applied to fix hair in shape, so it is something applied to set a hairdo.

clue.text: Welcome athletic achievement by one showing a bit of a leg

parts.note: hi is a greeting
PB is a personal best
one, placed by the rest

explanation.surface: A cheer for an athlete's feat by a competitor flashing some leg.
explanation.walkthrough: PB, personal best, is the athlete's term for their best-ever time or distance.
explanation.definitionFit: The hipbone is where the thigh joins the body, so it is loosely part of the upper leg.

clue.text: Buy bigger piano as addition to jazz and country club?

indicators.note: an addition is tacked on at the end, so this piece follows the others

parts.note: trad is traditional jazz
the European Union is a club of countries
p is the musical marking for piano, softly

explanation.surface: A golf club buys a grander piano to go with its jazz nights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country club' looks like a golf club; it is a club made of countries. The question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: To trade up is to swap something for a larger or more expensive version, such as a bigger house or car.

clue.text: Coat with a small amount of white spirit?

parts.note: pale means whitish, lacking colour
a tot is a small measure of drink
surface padding that says what the small measure is of, a nip of liquor

explanation.surface: Something coated with a drop of white spirit, the paint thinner.
explanation.walkthrough: White spirit is a paint solvent, which hides the drink; the question mark flags that a pale tot is a measure of clear spirit such as gin.
explanation.definitionFit: A paletot is a loose outer overcoat, a rare borrowing from French in dictionaries.

clue.text: Wife who survived a year with bishop

parts.note: p.a. means per annum, so a year
RR is Right Reverend, a bishop's title

explanation.surface: A woman lived another twelve months with the help of a clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry VIII's six wives were divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived; Catherine Parr was the one who outlived him.
explanation.definitionFit: Catherine Parr was the sixth and last queen of Henry VIII, the only spouse still alive when the king died.

clue.text: Pressure put on US mobile psychiatric unit facility

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure
added on, as weight is put on
Americans call a mobile phone a cell

explanation.surface: Stress being heaped on an American mobile mental health team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile psychiatric unit' reads as one phrase, but 'US mobile' is the phone and the definition starts after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Psychiatric hospitals once had rooms with cushioned walls to stop disturbed patients injuring themselves.

clue.text: Departs stern and miserable

parts.note: d. is the timetable abbreviation for departs
the stern is the rear of a ship

explanation.surface: Someone leaves looking severe and unhappy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stern' looks like an adjective next to miserable; it is the back of a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: Drear is a poetic form of dreary, meaning dismal, gloomy and cheerless.

clue.text: Algae from half of lake unexplored up in the middle

parts.note: the second half

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top
half of a word keeps only part of it, here its back end
the centre of a word gives just its central pair

parts.note: the central two of ten letters

explanation.surface: Seaweed taken from part of a lake nobody has yet explored.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the middle pair is turned upwards; the half of 'lake' stays as it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Kelp is a large brown seaweed, and seaweeds are marine algae, so the definition is a category.

clue.text: Perversely, went for another ending to latest film

indicators.note: doing something perversely means doing it the wrong way round, so the letters are disordered

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: an ending is the final part, so only the last letter counts

parts.note: the final letter

explanation.surface: A director stubbornly chose an alternative ending for their newest movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For' does double duty in the surface; the fodder is 'went' plus 'another' with 'for' between them, all shuffled with the final T.
explanation.definitionFit: On the Waterfront is the 1954 Marlon Brando picture about corruption among dock workers.

clue.text: I might be carried off when picked up

indicators.note: picking up a signal means hearing it, so the word is judged by sound

parts.note: to carry off a prize is to win it

explanation.surface: A person fears being kidnapped if someone gathers them up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' looks like the speaker but is the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman numeral I stands for the number one, the lowest counting number.

clue.text: Partner once having had a vacation cut short is free

indicators.note: cutting something short trims its end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: an ex is a former partner
vacating a place leaves it with nobody in it

explanation.surface: A former spouse whose holiday was curtailed is now at liberty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vacation' reads as the American word for a holiday; it is the act of vacating, leaving a place bare.
explanation.definitionFit: Exempt means excused from a duty or charge, so someone exempt is free of that obligation.

clue.text: Most idiotic time to take short bow, on reflection

indicators.note: a mirror reflection shows things back to front
something short is missing its end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
to take is to seize
a bow is curved, an arc

explanation.surface: It is foolish to take a quick bow and think about it afterwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bow' looks like a curtsy; it is a curve. Everything is strung together and then read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Crazy can mean foolish or senseless, so the superlative describes the most stupid or absurd of all.
